lines: I remember being rubble. You helped set the first stone back in place.
The cure cracked the old dark apart. You were there when the wall held.
You set me back into myself one careful piece at a time.
The first thing I recognized was your voice telling me to hold on.
I woke cold and weak, but I knew I was myself again.
You saw a villager under all that sickness. Thank you.
My hands stopped shaking before my memories settled. You stayed through both.
I remember the cure hurting, then the room becoming real again.
The village gave me my bed back. You gave me the chance to use it.
I owe you more than cheaper stone and a polite nod.
I touched the workshop wall after I woke just to feel something familiar.
Bread tasted ordinary again. I did not know how much I missed ordinary.
My family says you checked on me until morning.
I still have bad dreams, but now I wake up at home.
You carried the risk while I could not even carry a cup.
I remember your face more clearly than I remember the hunger.
The stonecutter sounded awful that first morning. I was glad to hear it.
I have my work, my neighbors, and my own thoughts again because of you.
If you ever need a strong wall, come to me first.
I am glad to see you. After what you did, that should not surprise you.
Your face is carved into that memory, but weather has worn it strange.
I remember stone-cold hands, a golden taste, and standing upright again.
The memory is worn smooth in places, but your hands are still carved into it.
Some parts of the cure are clear. The rest feel buried under rubble.
Your voice sounds familiar before the words do.
I know I should thank you. I am still fitting the reason together.
Did you hold the cup, or were you the one keeping me still?
I remember iron bars more clearly than the room outside them.
My mind keeps handing the days back in the wrong order.
There is a blank place in my memory with your face at the edge of it.
I woke knowing the stonecutter and not knowing half the people around me.
Please tell me your name again. I want it to stay this time.
I remember being terribly hungry, then too weak to lift my head.
Was I trying to hurt you? Nobody answers that gently.
The fever is gone, but it left cracks in the story.
I recognize the worry on your face. I must have seen it before.
Some mornings I remember the cure. Today I only remember waking.
Tell me what happened slowly. I would rather know than guess.
I am grateful even if I cannot yet remember every reason.
Whatever you did, I came back safe. That much is solid.
I remember you from beneath a collapsed roof of thoughts. Speak gently.
That cure left dust in the corners of my mind. Move carefully around it.
I know you helped, but the memory still sounds like falling stone.
I am grateful. I am also afraid. Both things are true.
Do not touch me without warning, even if you mean well.
I remember the bars, the hunger, and your voice outside it all.
You did what had to be done. It still felt terrible from where I was.
Give me room to breathe before you ask how I am.
I woke as myself, but my body still expected the cage.
The sound of a bottle opening can bring the whole night back.
I believe the village when they say you saved me.
Part of me trusts you. The rest is taking longer.
Please do not make a public story out of what happened.
I can thank you from here. Here is a good distance.
Some memories return like loose stone underfoot.
I am not angry with you. I am angry that any of it happened.
Leave the way out clear while we talk.
The old <shake>groan</shake> still follows me into sleep.
I may be steadier the next time you see me.
You gave me my life back. I need time to feel safe inside it.
